genotype-phenotype.def: Genotype is the set of alleles a person carries for a gene or trait; phenotype is what is expressed and can be observed or measured, such as a blood type or a disease. Phenotype depends on genotype and environment. A trait is any inherited characteristic.

allele.def: One version of a gene. A person with two identical alleles of a gene is homozygous; with two different alleles, heterozygous. A gene with multiple alleles, such as ABO, has more than two versions in the population, though each person carries only two.

dominance.def: A dominant allele shows its effect with one copy; a recessive allele only with two. A carrier is a healthy heterozygote with one recessive disease allele. Autosomal dominant and recessive patterns involve genes on autosomes; a recessive lethal allele kills only homozygotes, a dominant lethal allele anyone with one copy.

punnett.def: A grid that lists every equally likely combination of two parents' gametes, giving the chance of each genotype in a child. It rests on Mendelian inheritance and the law of segregation: each gamete carries one allele of each gene, each with a 1 in 2 chance.

codominance.def: In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote's phenotype falls between the two homozygotes'. In codominance, the heterozygote fully expresses both alleles, as in blood type AB, where A and B are codominant.

sex-linked.def: Inheritance of genes on the X chromosome. Males have one X, so an X-linked recessive allele, such as the one for hemophilia A, shows in any male who has it and passes from carrier mothers to half their sons; an X-linked dominant allele shows with one copy in either sex.

polygenic.def: Inheritance of a trait shaped by many genes, each with a small effect, plus the environment, such as height or blood pressure. It gives a continuous, bell-shaped range rather than distinct types.

chromosomal-disorders.def: Disorders caused by an extra, missing or rearranged chromosome, seen on a karyotype (the chromosomes photographed in metaphase and arranged in pairs). A trisomy is three copies of one chromosome; trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome, whose risk rises with maternal age.
